title: TB4-08549
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: This is the decision of the Refugee Protection Division in the matter of the Application to Vacate the decision of the Division of November 29, 1995, to grant refugee protection to XXXX XXXX XXXX BACKGROUND

On XXXX XXXX, 1995, the respondent entered Canada using an unknown Nigerian passport at Lester B. Pearson International Airport and made a claim for refugee protection. On June 16, 1995, the respondent signed his Personal Information Form (PIF)1 affirming that the information he provided is true and correct.

The claimant, in his PIF narrative provided that he was a member of a pro-democracy and human rights group in Nigeria known as the Campaign for Democracy. The claimant stated that he joined the organization in 1992 and prior to that he was a member of the Social Democratic Party.

During the 1993 elections, the claimant was involved in several protests over the government's decision to annul the election results after the candidate for the claimant's party had been believed to have won the election. The claimant reported that he was actively involved in mobilizing protesters and preparing placards for the demonstrations.

On XXXX XXXX, 1994, the claimant was attacked at his home by members of the Nigerian army and shot in the XXXX. The claimant fled to XXXX where he obtained the help from a traditional healer and remained in hiding until he could flee Nigeria.

On September 5, 2014, the Minister made an Application to Vacate the refugee protection granted to the claimant, pursuant to section 109(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act2 and pursuant to Rule 57 of the previous Refugee Protection Division Rules. At the same time, the Minister disclosed the evidence to be relied upon to support the Application.

The Application is under section 109 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act ("the Act"), which provides as follows: (1) The Refugee Protection Division may, on application by the Minister, vacate a decision to allow a claim for refugee protection, if it finds that the decision was obtained as a result of directly or indirectly misrepresenting or withholding material facts relating to a relevant matter. (2) The Refugee Protection Division may reject the application if it is satisfied that other sufficient evidence was considered at the time of the first determination to justify refugee protection. (3) If the application is allowed, the claim of the person is deemed to be rejected and the decision that led to the conferral of refugee protection is nullified.

According to the Minister's evidence, the claimant directly or indirectly misrepresented or withheld material facts relating to a relevant matter. The specifics of the Minister's allegations is that the respondent withheld a material fact in that he used an altered passport to enter the United States of America (US) prior to making his refugee claim in Canada, under another name and a visa in someone else's name which he failed to disclose at his original hearing. According to the Minister, this omission relates to the relevant matter of possible exclusion under Article 1F(b) of the Convention, relating to serious criminality prior to entering the country of refuge.

According to the Minister's submissions, the claimant entered Canada on XXXX XXXX, 1995, at Lester B. Pearson Airport in Toronto using an unknown Nigerian passport. At the time of his entry, the respondent held himself out to be a citizen of Nigeria and no other country. At the time of his claim, he reported that he was being sought by the Nigerian police and military.3

In XXXX 1987 in Indianapolis, Indiana, the respondent was questioned by US Immigration authorities. At the time of the interview, the respondent was told by the officers that the passport he was using had a visa which does not belong in it and that the 17th page of the passport had been removed and the visa belonging to another person had been put in its place. The information contained in this visa pertained to a female that the respondent claimed not to know. It was also brought to light that the photograph in the passport had been changed.4

According to the Minister's submissions, the use of a fraudulent or falsified document has a maximum sentence of ten years pursuant to Section 368 of the Criminal Code of Canada.5 The Minister submits that the respondent could have been excluded had he disclosed his use of a fraudulent document to the original panel. The penalty for said offence carries a maximum penalty of ten years imprisonment and is considered a serious crime in Canada.

The Minister further submits that the material facts the respondent misrepresented and withheld are so material as to call into question the credibility of the respondent's account for fearing persecution. THE HEARING and PROCEDURAL ISSUES

The initial hearing for this application was scheduled on November 24, 2014. While counsel for the Minister was present at the first sitting, the respondent was not. The panel questioned Minister's counsel on her efforts to locate and serve their application on the respondent. Although the panel was satisfied as to the steps taken by the Minister given that the respondent's address appeared to be current, the panel adjourned the hearing to allow a second notice and Minister's disclosure to be served upon the respondent out of fairness to the respondent and for the purposes of natural justice. A resumption date was set for January 20, 2015.

At the second sitting on January 20, 2015, the respondent was not in attendance. The panel adjourned the hearing for a break and instructed counsel for the Minister to verify their databases to verify if they had any updated information in regards to the respondent's address or whereabouts. After returning from the break, the panel was informed by Minister's counsel that they did not have any new or updated information.

Further to this, the panel was made aware by Minister's counsel that their disclosure had been successfully delivered to the respondent on November 25, 2014, however, the Immigration and Refugee Board's Notice to Appear for the hearing was returned on January 9, 2015.

Given the efforts made by both the IRB and Minister's counsel, the panel was satisfied that reasonable efforts had been made in trying to locate and contact the respondent and continued with the hearing on January 20, 2015.
At the hearing, Minister's counsel outlined their case and presented their submissions in regards to the Application to Vacate the Refugee Protection Division's November 29, 1995 decision.

Therefore in the analysis of the minister's application the following factor or question had to be considered: Was there a misrepresentation or withholding of material facts and whether this misrepresentation related to a relevant matter? In reviewing the evidence provided, the previous RPD file had been destroyed given the passage of time. According to Minister's counsel, she had copies of the audio cassettes which were not included as evidence or on hand at the Board. Given that the respondent was not in attendance, the panel therefore relied on the Minister's disclosure, namely the PIF and Minister's exhibits in assessing this application.

The panel agrees with Minister's counsel and finds that the claimant did misrepresent material facts relating to relevant matters. According to the PIF submitted and signed by the respondent, in answer to question 21 which asks "Have you ever committed or been convicted of any crime or offence in any country?" the respondent checked off the answer "No" and answered "See answer to Q. 37".

In reviewing question 37 of the respondent's PIF, question 37 is the claimant's narrative. Having reviewed the narrative, there is no mention of the respondent's having used an altered passport to try and gain entry or status in the US. In fact there are no references whatsoever at question 37 about the respondent having travelled to or entered the US, therefore the panel believes that he was referring to his activities in Nigeria when he answered question 21 and omitted the events that occurred in the US.

The panel then went on to review the other areas of the respondent's PIF to determine if there was any mention of his having been in the US or had any dealings with immigration officials there. According to Question 18 of his PIF, the respondent stated that he worked as a XXXX for the XXXX XXXX XXXX from XXXX 1983 until XXXX of 1985. He then answered further down that he worked as an XXXX in Rhode Island from XXXX 1987 until XXXX 1989. At question 22 of the PIF, he completed that from 1986 until XXXX 1989 he was an illegal immigrant in Rhode Island and further down he wrote from 1983 to 1985 he was a visitor and illegal immigrant in Houston, Texas.

As it relates to documents, the respondent provided at questions 28 and 29 that his Nigerian passport had been taken by the agent, however, he did have his Rhode Island driver's license and copy of his Marriage Certificate issued by the state of Ohio.

At question 34, it asks "Have you ever been to Canada before?" to which the respondent answered "yes" in 1987 "Transit to USA". Throughout the PIF, the panel confirmed that there was no mention of the respondent's issues or dealings with US immigration authorities or his use of the altered passport as alleged by the Minister.

Further to this, the panel was presented with the respondent's dealings with US immigration officials and specifically the interview notes and results of his attempt to use the altered passport to gain entry and status in the US. In reviewing the Record of Sworn Statement by the US Department of Justice as well as the Memorandum at page 25 of the Minister's evidence, the concerns of the examining officer in regards to the passport are clearly explained as to why they believe the passport to have been altered and the issues surrounding the visa having been issued to another person yet found inside the respondent's passport.

The Minister's evidence found at pages 26 and 27 completed by the US Department of Justice outline the allegations and reasons for the respondent being detained pending an inquiry by an immigration judge. These facts also do not appear to have been disclosed by the respondent in his PIF. According to notes found at page 28 of the Minister's evidence, the US authorities were considering their options at the time and states: "The subject's file was reviewed by AUSA XXXX XXXXat the Indianapolis INS office and it was decided that pending the outcome of the Immigration hearing, no decision would be made concerning prosecution at this time. AUSA XXXX stated that if the SUBJECT was found excludable and deportable then his office would most likely decline prosecution. XXXX also stated that if for any reason the SUBJECT was not deported then he would like to review the file again and he would most likely take the case for prosecution. If the SUBJECT is not found deportable or excludable, please notify the Indianapolis INS office so that appropriate action may be taken."

The Minister also submitted a forensic analysis of the passport in question completed by the INS' Forensic Document Laboratory and found at page 30 of the Minister's disclosure. In reviewing the forensic report, the conclusion of the analyst is that page 17 of the original passport was removed and replaced with a different page 17. The photograph at page 3 points to irregularities but is inconclusive of finding it to be a photo substitute. In regards to the signature, the analyst was requesting additional signatures from the respondent in order to conduct a more comprehensive analysis.

At page 31 of the Minister's evidence is correspondence from the Attorney General's office in Chicago, Illinois, to the US Embassy in Lagos' Immigrant Visa Section. The correspondence outlines the attempted use of an altered Nigerian passport by the respondent in an effort to gain entry or status in the US.

Further to this evidence the panel was also presented with documents from the US Department of Justice Order to Show Cause, Notice of Hearing, and Warrant for Arrest of Alien dated XXXX XXXX, 1989 (found at page 34 of the Minister's evidence). The following page refers to the Record of a Deportable Alien and refers to the respondent and his address in Rhode Island. The same report provides physical descriptors. According to his immigration record it states "Granted V/R withdrew application for admission arrested by No. Prov P.D. for XXXX XXXX XXXX."6
Further below, it notes that the respondent was convicted with remarks that state that the respondent was arrested and released on bail. "Subject was arrested for XXXX and for several XXXX XXXX."7

While this offence was not raised by the Minister as offences for which the respondent could have been excluded, the panel nonetheless notes that these dealings with US authorities and crimes for which he appeared to have been charged with were also omitted from the respondent's PIF. On page 39 of the Minister's evidence is a Warrant for Deportation signed by the US Department of Justice's District Director and dated XXXX XXXX, 1989. The final document from the US authorities is correspondence from counsel for the respondent, XXXX XXXX to the US INS stating that his client, the respondent left the US and returned to Nigeria on XXXX XXXX, 1989. Counsel for the respondent stated that he instructed his client to contact the US Embassy in Lagos in order to confirm his departure.

At page 42 and 43 of the Minister's evidence is a criminal records check on the respondent with the US authorities. According to the results, XXXX XXXX is one of nine aliases for an individual named XXXX XXXX XXXX. This same record notes five different dates of birth and two different social security numbers.

The following page of the criminal records check (page 43) again refers to the respondent as an alias for the person named XXXX XXXX XXXX. According to the results, the name XXXX XXXX a.k.a. XXXX XXXX was under deportation proceedings with both the Rhode Island INS office and Boston INS field offices. The original record for XXXX XXXX XXXX referred to an arrest by the Houston INS Field Office in 1983.

Given the evidence above, the panel finds that the claimant misrepresented or withheld material facts relating to a relevant matter. Specifically, he did not disclose his use of an altered passport in an attempt to gain entry and status in the United States for which the Minister is alleging would have led to there being serious reasons for considering that he could have been excluded by the panel of first instance.

As it relates to the issue of exclusion under Article 1F(b), there must be serious reasons for considering that the claimant, or in this case, the respondent committed a serious non-political crime outside the receiving country. In this case, the panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the respondent did in fact use an altered passport in an effort to gain entry and status in the US. If committed in Canada, these actions or offences would be equated to the offence as alleged by the Minister, that being pursuant to section 368 of the Criminal Code of Canada for Using, Trafficking or Possession of a Forged Document.

Section 368 states: 368. (1) Everyone commits an offence who, knowing or believing that a document is forged, (a) Uses, deals with or acts on it as if it were genuine; (b) Causes or attempts to cause any person to use, deal with or act on it as if it were genuine; (c) Transfers, sells or offers to sell it or make it available, to any person, knowing that or being reckless as to whether an offence will be committed under paragraph (a) or (b); or (d) Possesses it with intent to commit an offence under any paragraphs (a) to (c) (1.1) Everyone who commits an offence under subsection (1) (a) is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to imprisonment for a term of not more than 10 years or; (b) is guilty of a summary offence punishable on summary conviction. (2) For the purposes of proceedings under this section, the place where a document was forged is not material.

Having assessed the actions of the respondent, the panel finds that he did not use the passport on his way to Canada for the purpose of making a refugee claim but in fact used it several years prior for the purpose of attempting to gain entry and status in the US.

The Federal Court has held that were the respondent to be excluded from refugee protection by the original panel, there is no obligation for the panel to assess whether there was any untainted or remaining evidence which could have justified or supported the decision of the original panel.8

Further to this, the panel also notes that the respondent did not disclose any of his criminal history in the US. Furthermore, the panel also finds that the number of associated aliases to this individual as found in the criminal records check could have led the panel of first instance to have serious concerns regarding the identity and credibility of the respondent and which could have been determinative in rejecting the claim.

In conclusion, it is the decision of this panel to vacate the decision to allow the claim for refugee protection, on the grounds that the decision was obtained as a result of the respondent directly or indirectly misrepresenting or withholding material facts relating to relevant matters, and that there was not sufficient evidence remaining before the original decision maker to justify the granting of refugee protection to the respondent.

The decision to allow XXXX XXXX XXXX refugee protection is vacated, his claim is deemed to be rejected, and the decision that led to the conferral of refugee protection is nullified. (signed) "C.
